analysis.one_liner: Lets college athletes earn money from endorsements using their name, image, and likeness.
analysis.headline: Introduced June 18, 2020 with no cosponsors, the bill died in the Senate Commerce Committee without a hearing or vote when the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the NCAA and any similar college sports governing body to set a policy letting college athletes sign endorsement deals and get paid for the use of their name, image, or likeness, and to hire an agent to help with those deals. Athletes would have to report the deals to their school and the governing body, and the rules would still be allowed to preserve 'amateur status.' The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the policy, states would be barred from passing their own athlete-pay laws, and no one could sue the NCAA over the rules it adopts.
analysis.who_benefits: College athletes, especially the football and basketball players whose names and images sell tickets and merchandise, could earn endorsement money from outside companies and hire agents to negotiate for them.

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires any intercollegiate athletic association, including the NCAA, to establish a policy permitting student athletes to earn compensation from third parties for use of their name, image, or likeness.
It would let student athletes obtain professional representation for such compensation, subject to the existing federal sports-agent law.
The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the requirement, including against nonprofit organizations, treating violations as unfair or deceptive practices.

analysis.who_pays: Colleges and their athletic departments, which currently control and profit from athletes' names, images, and likenesses, would lose that exclusive control, and the NCAA would lose some rulemaking discretion over athlete earnings.
analysis.who_pays_short: College athletic departments and the NCAA

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves the rules for preserving 'amateur status' to the athletic associations themselves, so the NCAA could still write restrictions on how much athletes earn and from whom.
It preempts all state laws on athlete compensation, overriding states that had already passed their own rules letting athletes be paid on broader terms.
It bars any lawsuit in court against the athletic association or its member schools over the policies they adopt, so athletes would have no legal recourse if the new rules favored the schools.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gives athletes a real new right to earn money, but it hands the NCAA a bargain in return: legal immunity for whatever rules it writes and a national preemption that wipes out stronger state laws like California's. Athletes would gain earning power while the association kept control of the terms. As drafted, the trade leaned toward protecting the institution as much as the athlete.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never scheduled a hearing or vote, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Marco Rubio introduced the bill in the Senate on June 18, 2020, and it had no cosponsors.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, where no further action was taken before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: College athletic departments and the NCAA, which kept the existing arrangement under which they, not the athletes, control and monetize athletes' names, images, and likenesses for the remainder of the Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: College sports institutions and the NCAA

for.name: Marco Rubio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate Commerce Committee.

against.name: Roger Wicker
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Committee took no action on the bill after referral; no hearing, markup, or floor vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: One Republican senator sponsored the bill with zero cosponsors from either party, and no vote was ever taken, so the record shows no partisan pattern.

industries.industry: NCAA and college sports governing bodies
industries.note: The bill would have forced the NCAA to let athletes earn endorsement money, but it also would have granted the association immunity from lawsuits over its rules and preempted stronger state laws, locking in its role as the sole rulemaker for college athletics.

Schools currently capture the licensing value of athletes' names and images; the bill would have cost them that revenue, though it also shielded them from lawsuits over whatever policies they adopted.
The bill explicitly allows athletes to hire professional representation for endorsement deals, expanding the agent market, while keeping agents subject to existing federal sports-agent regulation.
Companies would gain a new market of college athletes available for endorsements; the bill also directs associations to write rules against third parties using deals to improperly recruit athletes.
